guideTitle: 6 Best Sock Aids After Hip Replacement in 2026
metaTitle: Best Sock Aids After Hip Replacement (2026)
metaDescription: Six sock aids and dressing kits compared on cord length, foot width, handle grip and compatibility, to help you get socks on without bending far forward.
introParagraphs: Putting on socks is one of the first everyday tasks that becomes awkward when bending forward is uncomfortable or restricted. A sock aid is a simple device: you slide a sock over a curved cradle, drop it to the floor, slip your foot in, and pull the cords or handles to draw the sock up. The idea is to reduce how far you need to reach, and the details of the cradle, the cords and the grip decide how easy that is.

This lineup covers six options, from basic one-piece aids to complete dressing kits with a reacher, a shoehorn and a leg lifter. Some are built for weak hand strength with soft foam handles, some use adjustable straps, and one is sized for a specific foot width. We describe the design intent of each product and not any medical outcome, and individual needs vary a lot.

Our assessment is based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on use. Surgeons and therapists give specific instructions about movement after hip surgery, and those instructions come first. A physical or occupational therapist can also recommend which dressing tools suit a particular person, including how to handle compression stockings.

products.name: RMS Deluxe Sock Aid with Foam Handles
products.description:
The RMS Deluxe uses a soft, flexible contoured plastic shell that holds a sock open while your foot slides in. Foam handles on the pull cords are designed for people with weak hand strength, because they are easier to hold than thin rope. The listing describes it as a daily living aid for putting on socks independently.

The shell flexes, which suits a range of foot shapes and makes insertion of the sock easier. It is not intended for compression socks, compression stockings or very thin hosiery such as sheer anklets, so check what you wear most often. That limit applies to most basic sock aids.

Setup is just choosing a seat where you can reach your foot to the floor. Compared with the Kekoy that limits foot width to 4 inches, the RMS offers a softer, more forgiving shell. Next to the Fruipbox with its adjustable straps, it is simpler, and many users find simple easier to learn.
products.bestFor: People with limited hand strength who wear regular socks.
pros: Foam handles are easy on weak hands
Flexible shell fits many foot shapes
Simple to learn with no adjustments
Soft contoured plastic is gentle on socks
cons: Not for compression or sheer socks
Plastic shell may crease if stored folded

products.name: CAidRE 3.93 Inch Wide Sock Aid
products.description:
The CAidRE is described as 3.93 inches wide, which gives the sock more room to open than very narrow cradles. An extended lip and a non-slip foam pad help the sock stay in place while you pull it on. The contoured design is meant to guide the foot into the sock with less bending and straining.

The listing says it works with ankle, flat, knee, calf, athletic and dress socks, and not with compression socks. That covers the most common everyday types, though anyone dependent on compression garments will need another solution. Its target audience includes seniors, pregnant women and post-surgery users.

In daily use it is easy to hold and quick to set up. Against the Kekoy, which is suited to feet up to 4 inches wide, the CAidRE trades a specific width limit for a wider cradle. It sits between the RMS Deluxe's soft shell and the more adjustable Fruipbox, and is worth a look if sock slippage has frustrated you.
products.bestFor: Users whose socks slip off narrow cradles or who have broader feet.
pros: 3.93 inch cradle opens socks wider
Extended lip keeps socks from slipping
Non-slip foam pad grips the sock
Handles ankle through knee-high socks
cons: Cord details are thin in the listing

products.name: KEKOY Sock Aid for Putting on Socks
products.description:
The KEKOY states that it suits foot widths of 4 inches or 10.2 centimeters or less. That sizing note is helpful because it tells you up front whether the aid will fit, which many listings leave unsaid. It is aimed at people with knee or hip replacement and others who want to avoid bending to put on socks.

The listing recommends regular socks such as ankle, flat and knee socks, and warns against compression stockings. It also mentions all types of socks in another bullet, so confirm with the seller what the intended range is. The width limit may exclude wider feet or very thick socks.

It is a practical option for people with average or narrow feet. Compared with the CAidRE at 3.93 inches wide, the KEKOY's published limit is a fit check rather than a cradle measure. Unlike the Fruipbox with adjustable straps, it keeps a basic design that works without setup.
products.bestFor: Average or narrow feet where a published width limit is reassuring.
pros: States foot width limit of 4 inches
Designed to avoid bending forward
Aimed at knee and hip replacement users
Basic layout works without adjustments
cons: Wider feet may not fit the cradle
Not for compression socks or stockings
Mixed notes on which socks work best

products.name: Fruipbox Double Anti-Slip Sock Aid
products.description:
The Fruipbox lets you place the sock on the cradle, slide the foot in and pull the straps. The straps use adjustable button slots, so the length can be set to your height and reach. That customization is rare among sock aids and helps people who find standard cords too short or long.

Double anti-slip padding is meant to hold the sock firmly while you pull. The added strap hardware means a few more parts to understand, but the setup is a one-time job. The listing emphasizes reducing bending and effort, not any clinical benefit.

Its adjustable length makes it more flexible than the RMS Deluxe, which has fixed foam handles. Compared with the OMGOD kit's rope, the Fruipbox gives you a measured way to tune reach. It suits households where taller or shorter users share one aid, or where reach changes over time.
products.bestFor: Taller or shorter users who need to tune strap length to their reach.
pros: Button clip slots set strap length
Double anti-slip pads hold the sock
Adjusts to different heights and reach
Simple pull-strap method with a cradle
cons: More parts to learn than a basic aid
Strap handles are thinner than foam
Fit with thick socks is unclear

products.name: OMGOD Sock Aid Kit with Long Shoe Horn
products.description:
The OMGOD kit bundles a sock aid with foam handles and a sturdy rope with a long handle shoehorn. Together they cover socks and the step that comes right after, getting a shoe on without bending. The shoehorn is described as extra-long and lightweight with a curved hook.

The pairing is practical for anyone who wants one purchase for both tasks. The tools are basic, so there is no reacher or leg lifter, and the kit is not a full hip kit. The listing frames it as an all-in-one mobility aid set for daily dressing challenges.

In use, the foam handles help with grip and the long shoehorn helps with shoes and boots. Compared with the Nourislif seven-piece kit, the OMGOD is smaller and simpler. Against the single-purpose RMS Deluxe it adds a shoehorn, so you do not need a second order.
products.bestFor: Someone who wants socks and shoes handled in one small bundle.
pros: Includes sock aid and long shoehorn
Foam handles with a sturdy rope
Curved hook shoehorn eases shoe entry
Smaller bundle than full hip kits
cons: No reacher or leg lifter included
Shoehorn may not suit every shoe style

products.name: Nourislif 7-Piece Hip Kit
products.description:
The Nourislif is a seven-piece set that includes a 33 inch reacher grabber, a 27 inch dressing stick, a 16.5 inch long shoehorn, a 45 inch sock aid and a 40 inch long leg lifter. The dressing stick has a protective vinyl coating on its push and pull hook. The grabber has an anti-slip jaw and an ergonomic handle.

Bundling these tools suits people who expect to need several ways to avoid bending. The 45 inch sock aid has long cords for reaching the foot from a seated position. The trade-off is that you receive tools you may not all use, and the kit takes storage space.

Compared with the OMGOD two-piece kit, the Nourislif covers far more tasks. Against single sock aids like the RMS Deluxe, it offers breadth over depth. Because individual recovery instructions vary, ask a therapist which pieces to use and which to skip.

buyingCriteria.explanation: Most basic sock aids are not made for compression socks, compression stockings or sheer hosiery, and the RMS Deluxe, CAidRE and KEKOY all say so. If compression garments are part of your routine, ask your surgeon or therapist how to put them on, since a standard aid may not work. Stretchier or slightly larger regular socks are generally easier to don. Do not force a compression garment over a standard cradle.

Cords or straps must reach from the cradle to your hands without a long stretch. The Nourislif's sock aid is 45 inches, while the Fruipbox lets you set length through button clips. A longer cord helps if you sit in a tall chair, while adjustable length helps if height or reach differs between users. Fixed cords like the RMS Deluxe's are fine if the length suits you.

Thin rope can bite into weaker hands. Foam handles, as on the RMS Deluxe and OMGOD kit, are easier to hold and gentler on the fingers. Loop handles give another way to grip if fingers are stiff. Choose the grip that matches your hand strength, not the one that looks neatest.

A cradle that is too narrow squeezes a wide foot, and one that is too wide may slip. The KEKOY lists a 4 inch foot width limit, and the CAidRE is 3.93 inches wide. Measure the widest part of your foot first and compare it with the listing. Flexible shells, such as the RMS Deluxe's, forgive small mismatches.

The sock must stay on the cradle while you slide your foot in. The CAidRE uses an extended lip and a non-slip foam pad, and the Fruipbox uses double anti-slip padding. Without these, thin socks can slide off as you pull. Check how each design holds the sock in place.

A single aid costs less and stores easily, while a kit covers several tasks. The OMGOD pairs a sock aid with a long shoehorn, and the Nourislif includes seven pieces with a 33 inch grabber. Decide which tasks you actually find difficult. A therapist can suggest which tools matter for your situation.

howWeEvaluated.title: Sock compatibility
howWeEvaluated.description: We read each listing for which socks it supports and which it excludes. The RMS Deluxe, CAidRE and KEKOY all exclude compression socks, which is a key limit. The CAidRE's list of ankle, knee and dress socks was noted as clear. Compatibility mattered most because it decides whether the aid works at all.

howWeEvaluated.title: Reach and cords
howWeEvaluated.description: We compared cord or strap length and how it can be changed. The Nourislif's 45 inch aid and the Fruipbox's adjustable straps lead here. Fixed foam handles on the RMS Deluxe were judged on grip comfort.

howWeEvaluated.title: Fit and grip
howWeEvaluated.description: We assessed cradle width, lips and anti-slip pads. The KEKOY's 4 inch width limit and the CAidRE's 3.93 inch cradle were compared against the Fruipbox's double pads. Fit guidance in the listing earned credit.

howWeEvaluated.title: Kit value
howWeEvaluated.description: We weighed what each kit adds. The OMGOD includes a shoehorn and the Nourislif adds a reacher, dressing stick and leg lifter. Extras were credited only when they fit real dressing tasks.

howWeEvaluated.title: Lineup positioning
howWeEvaluated.description: We placed each pick so the six cover distinct needs. The RMS Deluxe leads on soft handles, the Fruipbox on adjustability, and the Nourislif on breadth. Findings are based on product specs and buyer feedback, not hands-on use.

faq.q: Do sock aids work with compression socks?
faq.a: Most basic sock aids do not, and the RMS Deluxe, CAidRE and KEKOY listings all say so. Compression garments are stiffer and may tear or fail to slide on a standard cradle. Ask your surgeon or therapist how to put them on. They can suggest alternatives made for that purpose.

faq.q: How long should the cords be?
faq.a: Long enough to reach your hands from the floor while seated comfortably. The Nourislif's sock aid is 45 inches, and the Fruipbox lets you adjust length. A tall chair needs longer cords than a low one. Test the reach before relying on it.

faq.q: Is a kit better than a single sock aid?
faq.a: It depends on which tasks are hard. A kit like the Nourislif adds a 33 inch reacher and leg lifter, which are useful only if you need them. If only socks are difficult, a single aid like the RMS Deluxe is simpler. A therapist can advise which pieces to buy.

faq.q: Will a sock aid fit a wide foot?
faq.a: Check the width in the listing. The KEKOY says 4 inches or less, and the CAidRE's cradle is 3.93 inches wide. Measure the widest part of your foot and compare. If in doubt, a flexible shell like the RMS Deluxe's gives more tolerance.

faq.q: Do I need to follow special instructions after surgery?
faq.a: Yes. Surgeons and therapists give specific movement guidance for each person, and a sock aid does not replace it. We describe design intent only. Always follow the instructions you were given first.

faq.q: How do I keep thin socks from slipping off?
faq.a: Choose an aid with an extended lip or anti-slip padding. The CAidRE has a lip and foam pad, and the Fruipbox has double anti-slip pads. Pull steadily instead of jerking. Slightly stretchier socks are generally easier to handle.

faq.q: How do I clean and store a sock aid?
faq.a: Wipe the shell with a damp cloth and let it dry. Keep the cords from tangling by hanging the aid or coiling it loosely. Store flexible shells flat to avoid creases. Check foam handles for wear and replace the aid if the shell cracks.
